blocks.text: …complete relaxation
Definition and purpose 🐕

Off-leash work is harmonious teamwork between us and our dog that is purposeful for the situation. It is the sum of all learned and established exercises that have been trained with trust and reliability.
Off-leash work is the culmination of all efforts so far and the measure of our training work with our dog.
In off-leash work we train bringing together the various skills, and our dog’s reliable coming to us.

Off-leash work is the culmination of all efforts so far and the measure of our training work with our dog.
In off-leash work we train bringing together the various skills, and our dog’s reliable coming to us.
Prerequisites 📋

Prerequisite: Once we have made established progress with our dog in basic training and are confident in everyday use of long-line training and distance interruptions, we can turn to the training content of off-leash work.
Equipment 🦮
For off-leash work we need a trailing line of about 6 metres in length.
A sturdy carabiner with a webbing that is easy to grip, not too heavy but hard-wearing, is recommended.
For safety reasons, no loops, rings or other restricting structures may be built into the trailing line.
Step 1: Training environment and getting started 🌿

The training sessions initially take place without distraction in open terrain, far from hazardous environmental conditions. As training progresses, we apply the training with increasing distraction – but always only in situations and under conditions that allow a successful outcome.

The training takes place while walking and should be integrated into daily routines. We therefore carry the training line with us every day and switch to it as soon as we reach suitable terrain away from the road.
In doing so, we make sure that bystanders are neither bothered nor endangered.
Step 2: Relaxed walking mode with a trailing line 🚶
We walk through the terrain in a relaxed way with our dog on the 6-metre line. Through long-line training, it has already learned to walk together with us in the close range most of the time.
As soon as our dog is in a relaxed walking mode, we let the trailing line out as far as possible without noticeably changing our walking rhythm. Everything should be very relaxed.
As long as our dog moves along with us in the close range, everything is fine.
Step 3: Conditioning the interruption with “Down” 📍

If the distance between us and our dog increases to the length of the trailing line, we calmly condition an interruption with a quiet “Down”. Under conditions unfavourable for this, such as unfamiliar strong distraction or difficult ground conditions, a “Sit” may be used instead.
The intermediate goal is for our dog to move along in our surroundings on a slack line and to be interrupted with “Down” when it reaches the boundary area.

To do this, we give the command “Down” and at the same time move briskly towards the dog, calmly repeating the command and adding a supporting hand signal (flat hand with a calm downward movement). Calmly taking hold of the line again prevents the dog from moving away from us and at the same time supports the dog’s increasing orientation in our direction over time.
Step 4: Waiting and walking on ⏱️
The dog now lies in front of us in “Down”. We let some time pass for the situation to calm down and set off again together with the dog.
To do this, we address our dog by name as relaxed as we possibly can and set off calmly. Our dog should then accompany us loosely again.
This procedure is now repeated throughout the entire time we walk together with our dog. If the dog stays within the slack-line range or does not strive purposefully away from us, everything is fine.
Step 5: Transition to the free-trailing line 🔓

Over the course of days and weeks, during phases when the dog is walking along with us particularly attentively, we can begin to drop the line casually. Our dog should not feel any change – we should under no circumstances address it in any special way. Everything should appear composed and normal.
Our dog may move fluidly within the off-leash work radius of about 6–10 metres. In the course of successful training, this radius may gradually be widened to a maximum of 20 metres.

An area larger than 20 metres is not practical: On the one hand, our influence on our dog diminishes rapidly; on the other hand, the risk increases that our dog registers suddenly occurring distraction stimuli well before we do, and we then have no chance to react quickly enough.
Step 6: Correction when leaving the working radius 🔄
If the dog lets itself be distracted and wants to move out of the trained area, we address it calmly and convincingly with “Down” while calmly taking hold of the end of the training line.
We briskly walk a few steps backwards and thereby support our dog in carrying out the required “Down” in our direction and so learning to turn away from its original direction.
Step 7: Long-term transition to no leash 📈

This procedure with the free-trailing line is now trained daily over weeks until we are established to the point that the “Down” procedure works even under constantly growing distraction and the long training line is ultimately no longer needed.

The transition from training with the trailing line to moving entirely without a leash ideally takes place over a longer period, in which we constantly alternate between holding the trailing line by hand and a freely trailing line that is no longer held, depending on the environmental variables we are moving in.

The phases in which we actively hold the trailing line should steadily decrease until we only walk with the line dropped. Little by little, the trailing line may then be shortened more and more, so that we approach the free-running state and can reliably secure our dog with “Down” in every distraction situation.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid tightening the trailing line during training.
Avoid switching too early to walking without an auxiliary line.
Avoid letting the dog operate in too large a radius too early and thereby becoming unable to act.
Avoid stress during practice.
Avoid loud communication.
Under all circumstances, avoid failed attempts and break-out actions that are successful for the dog, i.e. running away.
Practical impulse: Patience is the key

Off-leash work is not a sprint but a marathon. Every day, deliberately alternate between a held and a free-trailing line – depending on the terrain and the distraction level. The moment you drop the line and your dog calmly walks on is the result of all the previous hours of training. Give yourself this time.
→ Do I enter off-leash work training in a harmonious and calm manner?
→ Has the basic training been established and trained over the long term?
→ Are we moving in clear and peaceful terrain?
→ Have I brought about a relaxed walking mode?
→ Did I always keep the training line long and slack?
→ Was the dog always placed in “Down” when it left the slack-line state?
→ Did I carry out the correction procedure calmly?
→ As training continues, do I casually drop the line often enough?
→ Do I remain consistent with the “Down” correction when the dog leaves the working radius?
→ Do I give the whole training the necessary time and attention?
→ Do I heed the alternation between a held and a free-trailing line?
→ Do I praise generously and affectionately at the end of the training procedure?
